citations.quote: For an integer $n\ge2$, put $T_n=\mathbb R^2/(n\mathbb Z)^2$, with horizontal circles $\alpha_i=\{y=i\}$ and vertical circles $\beta_j=\{x=j\}$ for $i,j\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$. A **toroidal grid diagram of grid number $n$** is a pair of disjoint sets $\mathbb O,\mathbb X$ of points in the open cells of this grid such that every row and every column contains exactly one point of each set. At each crossing of the projected link, the vertical segment is over and the horizontal segment is under. Orient each horizontal segment from its $O$-marking to its $X$-marking and each vertical segment from its $X$-marking to its $O$-marking. The markings and these segments determine an oriented link. Following each component from an $O$ along its row to an $X$ and then along that column to the next $O$ defines a permutation of the $n$ $O$-markings; its cycles are the link components. The grid represents a knot precisely when this permutation is one $n$-cycle.

derivations.claim: Each $I(P,Q)$ is an integer count. For $P=Q$, $J(P,P)=I(P,P)$, so the two self-pair terms in the formulas for $M_{\mathbb O}$ and $M_{\mathbb X}$ are integers; the cross terms occur doubled. Hence both Maslov functions are integer-valued.

Suppose a rectangle $r$ is contained in the chosen fundamental square. Write its southwest and northeast corners as $x_1,x_2\in\mathbf x$ and its northwest and southeast corners as $y_1,y_2\in\mathbf y$; all other state points are common. In $J(\mathbf x,\mathbf x)-J(\mathbf y,\mathbf y)$ the common-point terms cancel, the ordered corner pair contributes $1$, and each point of $\mathbf x$ strictly inside $r$ contributes twice, once against each changed corner. Thus this difference is $1+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. In $2J(\mathbf x,\mathbb O)-2J(\mathbf y,\mathbb O)$ the same cancellation leaves twice the number of $O$-markings in $r$. Substituting these two counts into [F1] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)+2\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)$. Replacing every $O$ by $X$ gives the stated formula for $M_{\mathbb X}$.

For two complementary rectangles $r$ and $r'$ with the same horizontal edges, let $v$ be their common width, counted in column strips. The one-$O$- and one-$X$-per-column conditions in [F2] give $n_{\mathbb O}(r)+n_{\mathbb O}(r')=v$ and $n_{\mathbb X}(r)+n_{\mathbb X}(r')=v$. The state has one point on each of these $v$ vertical circles; the two endpoint corners are excluded from both interiors, so $\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r)+\#(\mathbf x\cap\operatorname{Int}r')=v-1$. If the formula of step 1.2 holds for $r$ from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$, these three equalities give the formula for $r'$ from $\mathbf y$ to $\mathbf x$ by subtraction. The same argument applies to complementary rectangles sharing vertical edges. Of the four torus rectangles for the two states, one lies in the fundamental square; successive horizontal or vertical complementations reach each of the other three, so the formulas hold for every torus rectangle.

Subtract the $M_{\mathbb X}$ change from the $M_{\mathbb O}$ change and divide by two. The constant terms and state-interior terms cancel, giving $\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x)}2-\frac{M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)-M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf y)}2=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The common normalization $-(n-1)/2$ in $A_G$ cancels, proving the rectangle-change formula and that all differences of $A_G$ are integers.

For a marking set $P\in\{\mathbb O,\mathbb X\}$, let $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P}$ be the grid state consisting of the northwest corners of the marked cells, with a corner on the top edge read on the identified bottom edge. Expanding the $J$ formula in [F1] gives
$$M_P(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}P})=\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}-\#\{(i,j):\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_j\}-\#\{(i,j):P_i<\mathrm{NW}(P_j)\}+\#\{(i,j):P_i<P_j\}+1.$$
For distinct $i,j$ neither mark in the top row, all four inequalities are equivalent and their signed contributions cancel. If $P_j$ is in the top row, the second and fourth inequalities are equivalent and the first and third are false; if $P_i$ is in the top row, the first and second inequalities are equivalent and the third and fourth are false. These contributions also cancel. For $i=j$, the only inequality that can hold is $\mathrm{NW}(P_i)<P_i$, and it holds exactly for the unique mark in the top row. The displayed count is therefore $-1+1=0$, proving $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})=M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X})=0$.

The row and column connections from $O$ to $X$ and back form one $n$-cycle by [F2]. Equivalently, the relative permutation between $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X}$ and $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O}$ is an $n$-cycle. Factor that cycle into $n-1$ transpositions and apply the transpositions successively to obtain a path of grid states between the two states; every transition is realized by a torus rectangle, whether empty or not. Each rectangle changes $M_{\mathbb X}$ by an odd integer by steps 1.2–1.3, so $M_{\mathbb X}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})\equiv n-1\pmod 2$, using the zero normalization at $\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb X}$ from step 2.2. Since $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})=0$, the numerator $M_{\mathbb O}-M_{\mathbb X}-(n-1)$ defining twice $A_G(\mathbf x_{\mathrm{NW}\mathbb O})$ is even. Hence this value is integral.

Any two grid states correspond to permutations, and a finite product of transpositions carries one to the other. Each transposition gives a rectangle transition. Step 2.1 shows that $A_G$ changes by an integer at every transition; since one state has integral Alexander value by step 2.3, all grid states do.

A **periodic domain** is an integral two-chain in the complementary regions whose boundary is an integral sum of full $\alpha$- and $\beta$-curves; its local multiplicity at a marked point is the coefficient of the containing region. derivations.claim: Let $p_{ij}$ be the coefficient of cell $R_{ij}$ in a periodic domain $P$. Because $\partial P$ is a sum of whole horizontal and vertical circles, the coefficient jump across a vertical circle is independent of the row, and the jump across a horizontal circle is independent of the column. Fix reference indices $i_0,j_0$ and set $a_i=p_{i,j_0}$ and $b_j=p_{i_0,j}-p_{i_0,j_0}$. Summing the constant jumps from the reference row and column gives $p_{ij}=a_i+b_j$ for every cell. Since the marking permutation in [F1] is one cycle, number its basepoint pairs in reverse order of knot travel so that row region $A_i$ contains $w_i,z_i$ and column region $B_i$ contains $w_i,z_{i+1}$, as allowed by the convention in [F2]. Then $P=\sum_i a_iA_i+\sum_i b_iB_i$, with local multiplicities $n_{w_i}(P)=a_i+b_i$ and $n_{z_i}(P)=a_i+b_{i-1}$.

Suppose $P$ is periodic and all $n_{w_i}(P)=0$. Then $b_i=-a_i$, so $n_{z_i}(P)=a_i-a_{i-1}$ and $\sum_i n_{z_i}(P)=0$. If one $n_{z_i}(P)$ is nonzero, these integer multiplicities include both a positive and a negative value; each is a region coefficient at the corresponding $X$-cell, so $P$ has both signs.

If all $n_{z_i}(P)$ also vanish, then all $a_i$ are the same integer $c$ and all $b_i=-c$. Hence $P=c(\sum_iA_i-\sum_iB_i)=0$, because each of the two sums is the whole torus with coefficient one. Thus a nonzero periodic domain with zero $O$-multiplicity cannot have all $X$-multiplicities zero, and step 1.2 proves it has both signs. By [F2], the grid diagram is admissible.

derivations.claim: For two successive rectangles $r_1,r_2$, let $\psi=r_1+r_2$ be their cellwise sum as a two-chain, and let $\mathbf x,\mathbf z$ be the initial and terminal states. The state permutation changes by one transposition at each rectangle. If $\mathbf x\ne\mathbf z$, their relative permutation is either a product of two disjoint transpositions, so four points move, or a $3$-cycle, so three points move. These are the only nonidentity products of two transpositions.

In the four-point case, the two transpositions are disjoint and commute. Exchanging their order gives the alternate intermediate state; the first rectangle in one decomposition has the same support as the second rectangle in the other, and conversely. Thus both decompositions have the same two rectangle interiors and are empty together. No third decomposition is possible, because the four distinct changing corners must be paired into the same two disjoint transpositions fixed by the endpoint permutation and the domain boundary.

In the three-point case, following the boundary of $\psi$ gives a six-corner region with five right-angle corners and one reflex corner of angle $270^\circ$; every cell coefficient is zero or one. At the reflex corner the boundary can be cut in exactly two ways into two rectangles. Each cut gives the required intermediate grid state, and the resulting interiors contain no additional state point because any such point would already lie in the interior of one of the original empty rectangles. The six-corner boundary has no other concave corner at which to make a cut, so these are exactly the two decompositions.

In either non-annular case the two decompositions have the same cellwise domain $\psi$. A forbidden $O$- or $X$-marking occurs in one rectangle of a decomposition exactly when its cell has positive coefficient in $\psi$; hence a mode excluding that marking accepts either both decompositions or neither. For each $O_i$, the exponent in the product coefficient is its multiplicity in $\psi$, so the two accepted terms have the same monomial. They cancel over $\mathbb F_2$.

If $\mathbf x=\mathbf z$, the two rectangles reverse the same state transposition and their union is a periodic annulus. If its width and height were both greater than one, the annulus interior would contain a state point on an intervening vertical or horizontal circle, contradicting emptiness. Thus the domain is one of the two thin annuli, of width one or height one. Each contains one $X$ in each column or row respectively, so it is excluded in tilde and associated-graded minus modes. In the full filtered minus mode each annulus contains every $O_i$ exactly once by [F1]; both contribute $\prod_{i=1}^nU_i$. The two annuli therefore cancel in characteristic two.

For a counted rectangle $r$ the interior contains no state point, so [F3] gives $M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf x)-M_{\mathbb O}(\mathbf y)=1-2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. The coefficient $\prod_iU_i^{O_i(r)}$ lowers Maslov degree by $2n_{\mathbb O}(r)$ by [F2]; hence the full term has degree $-1$.

The Alexander change in [F3] is $A_G(\mathbf x)-A_G(\mathbf y)=n_{\mathbb X}(r)-n_{\mathbb O}(r)$. Multiplication by the coefficient lowers filtration by $n_{\mathbb O}(r)$, so the output filtration is $A_G(\mathbf x)-n_{\mathbb X}(r)$. Thus the full filtered term drops by exactly $n_{\mathbb X}(r)$, and the tilde and associated-graded modes, which count only rectangles with $n_{\mathbb X}(r)=0$, preserve Alexander grading.

citations.quote: The **grid-complex algorithm** takes a finite encoded grid and a mode from $\{\mathrm{tilde},\mathrm{minus\text{-}associated\text{-}graded},\mathrm{minus\text{-}filtered}\}$. It requires an integer grid number $n\ge2$, disjoint $O$- and $X$-markings with exactly one of each in every row and column, and an induced component permutation that is one $n$-cycle. If $n<2$ or the marking conditions fail, return `invalid-grid`; if the component permutation has more than one cycle, return `link-input-not-supported`. No chain complex is returned on either branch.

A **grid state** is a subset $\mathbf x\subset\bigcup_{i,j}(\alpha_i\cap\beta_j)$ containing exactly one intersection on each horizontal and each vertical circle. After numbering the circles, grid states correspond bijectively to permutations of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, so there are $n!$ states. For states $\mathbf x,\mathbf y$, a **rectangle from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$** is an embedded torus rectangle whose sides lie in grid circles, whose northeast and southwest corners lie in $\mathbf x$, whose northwest and southeast corners lie in $\mathbf y$, and whose remaining state points agree. Rectangles are subsets of the torus, so their lifts may cross a chosen fundamental-domain edge. Such a rectangle is **empty** when its interior contains no point of $\mathbf x$; write $\operatorname{Rect}^{\circ}(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ for the empty rectangles from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y$.

derivations.claim: The validation stage scans the finite $n\times n$ marking array, counts the markings in each row and column, and traces a permutation on the finite set of $n$ markings. Each scan and each cycle check terminates. A failed size, marking, or disjointness condition returns `invalid-grid`; a valid marking array with more than one component cycle returns `link-input-not-supported`, exactly the two specified rejection branches.

On a valid knot input, the algorithm enumerates the $n!$ permutations. There are finitely many ordered state pairs; a pair has at most two candidate torus rectangles by [F2]. Testing whether a candidate is empty and counting its finitely many markings takes finitely many array operations. Every mode filter and coefficient calculation is therefore finite, so all matrix entries and grading lists are produced in finite time.

By [F2], every grid state appears exactly once in the permutation enumeration and every rectangle from a pair is among the enumerated torus rectangles. The empty-state test is the definition of $\operatorname{Rect}^{\circ}$; the mode-specific marking test and coefficient are the instructions in [F1]. Summing the accepted terms modulo two therefore gives exactly the specified differential matrix, and the remaining output fields are computed from the stated grading formulas.
